storySeeds.notes: M81 stirs M82 into a starburst (CAUSE); M51's companion sculpts crisp arms; M63 shows a spiral with no companion; M101 closes on surface brightness. storySeeds.title: A window out of the Milky Way (Coma Berenices)
storySeeds.notes: Look up out of the disk near the north Galactic pole: a dissolving nearby cluster (280 ly) → a halo globular (60,000 ly) → a galaxy (~15 Mly) → back to M3 as a richer globular. Each step 100–1,000× farther. Span ~22°.

card.question: How can missing stars tell a cluster’s age?
card.answer: The gaps are the clock: the heavy blue stars have all burned out while the next heaviest are only now swelling into giants, a moment that comes roughly 600 to 700 million years after birth.
card.glance: A swarm of several dozen stars, wider than the full Moon, in the dim patch of sky between Gemini and Leo.
card.whyHere: The Beehive is a star family in middle age, one of the finest binocular clusters in the sky.
card.see: Look midway between Pollux and Regulus, in faint Cancer, for a smudge visible to the eye on a dark night. Binoculars break it into dozens of white and pale-yellow stars in little triangles and pairs; hunt for a few warmer, yellow-orange points.
card.understand: All these stars were born together about 600 light-years away, and Gaia counts more than 1,300 of them. The heaviest, bluest stars run out of fuel first, and here they are long gone; the brightest survivors are white stars a few times the Sun’s mass, plus a handful of orange giants that have just begun to swell. One survivor, the binary ε Cancri, has been weighed with an interferometer, and its two stars pin the age at about 637 million years.
card.wonder: In 2012 giant planets were found circling two of its stars, the first known around Sun-like stars in a cluster.
card.connect: A short hop south, M67 is a family nearly as old as the Sun.
card.photoCaption: Survey photo of the full cluster; binoculars show crisper points and a little more color than this plate.
card.notSee: No glowing gas and no bright blue stars: what you see is all there is.
card.deeper: Gaia DR3 membership (Hunt & Reffert 2024) puts Praesepe at 183.5 pc with about 1,300 members and roughly 950 solar masses inside its tidal radius. Ages depend on method and model physics: published values run from about 590 to 790 Myr, and the interferometric binary ε Cancri gives 637 ± 19 Myr (Morales et al. 2022). Quinn et al. (2012) found hot Jupiters around the members Pr0201 and Pr0211 by radial velocity, with periods of 4.4 and 2.1 days. Its age and space motion resemble the Hyades, which has led to suggestions of a shared origin.

card.question: Can a star cluster survive for billions of years?
card.answer: Rarely, but M67 has, while most star families break apart within a few hundred million years.
card.glance: A soft, grainy glow about the size of the full Moon, with a few faint stars sparkling on top.
card.whyHere: M67 looks like a modest misty patch south of the Beehive, but its stars are close cousins of the Sun.
card.see: From Acubens, the star at the bottom of Cancer south of the Beehive, drift about two degrees west. M67 is a misty patch peppered with a handful of faint stars, smaller and dimmer than the Beehive because it is more than four times farther away.
card.understand: Its heavier stars died long ago, so its brightest survivors are yellow and orange giants, stars a little heavier than the Sun that have used up the hydrogen in their cores. Its age comes from an elegant comparison: astronomers found stars in M67 that are near-perfect twins of the Sun and compared their spectra with the Sun’s own, which gives about four billion years. That makes the cluster a family album of stars much like the Sun at nearly its present age.
card.wonder: Odd stars called blue stragglers live here too, stars that look too young because they gained mass from a partner or formed in a merger.
card.connect: Stars like these will eventually shed their outer layers, a gentle ending on display in the Owl Nebula.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo resolves hundreds of faint members that 50 mm binoculars merge into haze.
card.notSee: Individual faint members and their colors: binoculars catch only the brightest dozen or so.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024) list 1,844 Gaia DR3 members at 837 pc and about 2,800 solar masses within the tidal radius. Their neural-network age (about 1.7 Gyr) is known to be biased low for old clusters, so the KB uses the solar-twin analysis of Castro et al. (2011): 3.87 (+0.55/−0.66) Gyr at solar metallicity. The cluster also contains blue stragglers, stars that look too young because they gained mass from a companion or formed in a merger.

card.question: Where does M48 fit on the cluster clock?
card.answer: It sits right in the middle: at about 420 million years it has lost its blue giants but kept a crowd of white stars, a family in its middle years.
card.glance: A rich spray of faint stars, nearly as wide as the full Moon, on the border of Hydra and Monoceros.
card.whyHere: M48 is a rich spray of stars that Messier logged in the wrong place, and its brightest members carry a clock.
card.see: Start at ζ Monocerotis, about 11 degrees south-east of Procyon, and sweep about three degrees south-south-east. In 10×50s roughly two dozen stars stand out of a misty background, richer on the eastern side, with no glow of gas.
card.understand: A young cluster’s brightest stars are hot blue giants, and as it ages those burn out one weight class at a time. In M48 the brightest remaining stars are white, a couple of times the Sun’s mass, and a few have already become yellow giants. A second clock agrees: its Sun-like stars have destroyed an amount of their fragile lithium that falls between the Pleiades and the Hyades.
card.wonder: Messier logged it in 1771 with a position several degrees off, and for over a century nobody knew which cluster he meant.
card.connect: The Beehive tells the same story a chapter later.
card.photoCaption: Survey photograph of the central swarm; binoculars show the same bright stars on a fainter haze.
card.deeper: Gaia DR3 (Hunt & Reffert 2024): 747 pc, 778 members and about 1,500 solar masses inside the tidal radius. WIYN spectroscopy shows a lithium pattern intermediate between the Pleiades and the Hyades/Praesepe, consistent with an age of 420 Myr (Sun et al. 2023). Messier's 1771 position was off in declination; Caroline Herschel found the cluster independently in 1783, and Oswald Thomas (1934) and T. F. Morris (1959) identified it with NGC 2548 (SEDS).

card.question: What happens to a star cluster over time?
card.answer: It slowly falls apart as the Milky Way’s tides keep tugging members away, and the Coma Star Cluster is already more stream than cluster, the fate of almost every star family.
card.glance: A loose scatter of a few dozen fairly bright stars spread over about five degrees, too big for telescopes and perfect for binoculars.
card.whyHere: The Coma Star Cluster is one of the nearest star families to us, close enough for Gaia to watch what is happening to it.
card.see: Look between Denebola and Cor Caroli for a faint glittery patch to the eye. Binoculars turn it into a sprawl of white stars across most of the field, and the orange star γ Comae at its northern edge is a foreground star.
card.understand: These stars were born together some 700 to 800 million years ago, but the family is only loosely held. Gaia measured the motions of the members and found two long streams of stars trailing ahead of and behind the cluster, like smoke drawn from a chimney. Only about 50 Suns’ worth of stars remain inside the region where the cluster’s own gravity still wins.
card.wonder: Gaia has found escaped members streaming roughly 160 light-years out on each side, far wider than the patch you see.
card.connect: Behind this cluster lies a clear window out of our galaxy, crowded with distant galaxies.
card.photoCaption: A wide survey field; binoculars show the same bright stars, which the plate renders as soft disks.
card.notSee: The tidal tails: they are a statistical result from Gaia motions, invisible to any eye.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024) place it at 85.25 pc (278 ly) with 271 Gaia members, but only about 50 solar masses remain inside its 5 pc tidal (Jacobi) radius, a sign of advanced dissolution. Tang et al. (2019) found leading and trailing tidal tails each about 50 pc long and an age of roughly 700–800 Myr, older than the 400–600 Myr often quoted. The cluster lies close to the north Galactic pole, so the view here points almost straight out of the Milky Way's disk.

card.question: Can you see another galaxy with binoculars?
card.answer: That oval haze is one, a whole spiral galaxy of billions of stars whose light left it about 12 million years ago.
card.glance: A small oval glow with a brighter center, about half a degree from the fainter streak of M82.
card.whyHere: Bode’s Galaxy is one of the brightest galaxies beyond our own neighborhood, and half of a pair locked in a gravitational dance.
card.see: Extend the line from Phecda through Dubhe, in the Big Dipper’s bowl, by the same distance again, near the faint star 24 Ursae Majoris. Brace the binoculars: M81 is an oval haze with a starlike core, and M82 shares the field as a thin silvery streak.
card.understand: This is a whole spiral galaxy, a disk of billions of stars like our Milky Way. Its distance comes from stars bright enough to pick out one by one: Cepheids, whose pulse reveals their true brightness, and the brightest red giants, which all top out at about the same brightness. Radio telescopes also see streams of gas linking it to M82, pulled out when the two swung close a few hundred million years ago.
card.wonder: In 1993 an amateur astronomer found a supernova in it that reached about magnitude 10.5, bright enough for a small telescope.
card.connect: Its smaller companion, M82, took the encounter far harder.
card.photoCaption: Long exposures reveal spiral arms and dust lanes; binoculars show only the bright core and inner disk.
card.notSee: The spiral arms: they need long exposures or a large telescope.
card.deeper: Distances from Cepheids and the tip of the red-giant branch cluster around 3.6 Mpc (NED-D median 3.63 Mpc). Radio maps of neutral hydrogen show tidal bridges linking M81, M82 and NGC 3077; stars and clusters in the M81–M82 bridge point to a tidal passage roughly 200–300 Myr ago (de Mello et al. 2008). NASA lists a central black hole of about 70 million solar masses. Supernova 1993J, found by amateur Francisco García Díaz, peaked near magnitude 10.5 (SEDS).

card.question: What happens to a galaxy after a close pass with a bigger one?
card.answer: It can burst into star birth: M81’s pull funneled gas into M82’s core, which now forms stars about ten times faster than our entire Milky Way.
card.glance: A thin, slightly mottled sliver of light, sharing the binocular field with rounder M81.
card.whyHere: The Cigar Galaxy has had a close brush with its big neighbor, M81, and it still bears the marks.
card.see: With M81 in view, look a little over half a degree north for a narrow streak about a third as long as the Moon is wide. On a steady, dark night it can look patchy along its length, a hint of its dust lanes.
card.understand: M82 is a disk galaxy seen edge-on. The encounter with M81 funneled gas into its center, where it collapsed into crowds of new star clusters, and dust warmed by all those young stars makes M82 the brightest galaxy in the sky at infrared wavelengths. The young stars, and the explosions of the heaviest ones, drive a wind that blows gas out above and below the disk, seen in photographs as red plumes.
card.wonder: In January 2014 a supernova flared in M82, bright enough to see in a small telescope.
card.connect: The Whirlpool, under the Big Dipper’s handle, shows the same sculpting in a face-on spiral.
card.photoCaption: Hubble's colors show glowing hydrogen streaming out of the core; binoculars show a gray sliver.
card.notSee: The red outflow plumes and individual star clusters.
card.deeper: TRGB distances put M82 at about 3.5 Mpc (Dalcanton et al. 2009, via NED-D). NASA describes its central star formation as about ten times the Milky Way's total rate. It is the brightest galaxy in the sky in the infrared and a strong radio source (3C 231). SN 2014J, a Type Ia, was discovered on 21 January 2014 by S. J. Fossey and peaked near magnitude 10.9 (SEDS). The tidal passage with M81 is dated at roughly 200–300 Myr ago from stellar populations in the HI bridge (de Mello et al. 2008); other studies give up to several hundred Myr.

card.question: What draws the spiral arms of the Whirlpool?
card.answer: The passing companion draws them, and the arms are not fixed structures at all but more like traffic jams, places where gas and stars slow and crowd together before moving on.
card.glance: A faint, round glow, perhaps with a smaller knot touching it, south-west of Alkaid.
card.whyHere: The Whirlpool is the first galaxy in which anyone saw spiral arms.
card.see: From Alkaid, the end of the Big Dipper’s handle, hop about three and a half degrees south-west. Under a dark sky M51 is a small hazy patch, its companion perhaps a slight bulge on one side; in suburban skies it often vanishes.
card.understand: M51 is a spiral galaxy seen face-on, about 28 million light-years away, a distance found from its brightest red giants. A small companion galaxy has been gliding past behind it, and Hubble images show it tucked behind the end of one arm. Its gravity sends waves through M51’s disk, and gas piling up in those waves forms new stars that outline the arms in blue.
card.wonder: Lord Rosse sketched its spiral by eye in 1845, decades before anyone knew spirals were galaxies.
card.connect: A few degrees away, M101 is an even bigger face-on spiral that is harder to see.
card.photoCaption: Long exposures show two curving arms and the companion; binoculars show a small gray glow.
card.notSee: Spiral arms and the bridge to the companion.
card.deeper: The tip-of-the-red-giant-branch distance is 8.58 Mpc (McQuinn et al. 2016, via NED-D). Hubble imaging shows the companion NGC 5195 passing behind the Whirlpool (ESA/Hubble heic0506a). Three supernovae (1994I, 2005cs and 2011dh) have been found in M51, two of them by amateurs (SEDS). Its OpenNGC surface brightness, 22.9 mag/arcsec², is about one magnitude brighter than M101's, which is why this smaller galaxy is the easier binocular target.

card.question: Why is a big, bright galaxy so hard to see?
card.answer: Its light is spread thin, and your eye detects contrast, not total light, so a galaxy as bright as a binocular star can still slip past unseen.
card.glance: A very faint, large round glow, almost as wide as the full Moon, that is easy to sweep right past.
card.whyHere: The Pinwheel is one of the biggest spirals near us, and one of the hardest to spot in binoculars.
card.see: Picture an equilateral triangle with Mizar and Alkaid, in the Big Dipper’s handle, as two corners; M101 sits just inside the third, to the north. Look slightly to one side and gently tap the binoculars, and a broad, ghostly brightening may appear.
card.understand: M101 is a spiral roughly 170,000 light-years across, nearly twice the Milky Way’s width, and Cepheids in its arms give its distance precisely. Its total light equals a star you could see in binoculars, but it is spread over an area nearly as big as the Moon. The same rule makes big faint nebulae harder than small bright ones.
card.wonder: In May 2023 an amateur in Japan spotted a supernova in one arm, seen about 22 million years after it happened.
card.connect: Its distance is known precisely thanks to a yardstick calibrated in another spiral nearby, M106.
card.photoCaption: Long exposures pile up the faint arms; binoculars at best show a large, soft glow around the core.
card.notSee: The arms and bright knots of star formation.
card.deeper: Hubble Cepheids give 6.71 Mpc (Riess et al. 2016, via NED-D) and the red-giant-branch tip about 6.9 Mpc. NASA quotes a diameter of about 170,000 ly; the 24′ OpenNGC isophote at 6.71 Mpc gives about 153,000 ly. Its OpenNGC surface brightness, 23.97 mag/arcsec², is one of the lowest among bright Messier galaxies. Two famous supernovae: SN 2011fe (Type Ia, about magnitude 9.9 at peak, SEDS) and SN 2023ixf (Type II), found by Koichi Itagaki on 19 May 2023 and studied from the first day (Hiramatsu et al. 2023).

card.question: Why does the Sombrero look like a hat?
card.answer: We see it almost edge-on, so a ring of dark dust cuts across that huge bright bulge like the brim of a hat.
card.glance: A small, bright spindle of light with a brighter middle, on the border of Virgo and Corvus.
card.whyHere: The Sombrero is an edge-on galaxy with a giant bulge and about ten times our galaxy’s number of globular clusters.
card.see: From δ Corvi, the north-east corner of the Crow south-west of Spica, sweep a little over five degrees north-north-east. M104 is a small spindle with a bright center; its dark dust lane is beyond most 50 mm binoculars.
card.understand: The bulge is enormous, a swarm of old stars around a black hole of several hundred million Suns, weighed from how fast the stars near the center move. Around it orbit roughly 2,000 globular clusters, ancient balls of stars like those that circle our own galaxy. In 1912 Vesto Slipher measured its spectrum and found it rushing away at about 1,000 kilometers per second, far too fast to belong to the Milky Way.
card.wonder: Slipher’s measurement was one of the first clues that the universe is expanding.
card.connect: Our own galaxy’s globular clusters are binocular targets too, and one waits in Hydra.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos show the knife-edge dust lane; binoculars show the bright bulge as a small spindle.
card.notSee: The dark dust lane and the halo of globulars.
card.deeper: TRGB distance 9.55 ± 0.13 Mpc (McQuinn et al. 2016, via NED-D), so it lies in front of the Virgo Cluster rather than in it. Orbit-based stellar-dynamical models give a central black hole of (6.6 ± 0.4) × 10⁸ solar masses (Jardel et al. 2011); older estimates were about 10⁹. NASA quotes nearly 2,000 globular clusters. Slipher's 1912 velocity of about 1,000 km/s was the first large redshift measured for a galaxy (SEDS).

card.question: How can you measure a galaxy’s distance with pure geometry?
card.answer: Watch something orbit and measure it two ways, as M106’s water clouds allow, and the distance falls out of geometry alone; astronomers then use it to calibrate Cepheids, the pulsing stars that reach much farther galaxies.
card.glance: A faint elongated glow with a slightly brighter middle, in empty-looking sky between the Big Dipper and Cor Caroli.
card.whyHere: M106 is the galaxy measured by pure geometry, a cornerstone for measuring the universe.
card.see: Sweep about halfway from Phecda, in the Big Dipper’s bowl, to Cor Caroli. Under dark skies M106 is a faint oval smear with a slightly brighter center, and bracing the binoculars helps.
card.understand: Deep in M106’s core, clouds of water molecules circle a black hole and beam out microwaves like natural lasers. Radio telescopes track them two ways: how fast they move, from the shift in their frequency, and how far they creep across the sky each year. A speed in kilometers and a drift in angle can only match at one distance, the same trick a surveyor uses, and it gives about 25 million light-years with an uncertainty of about 1.5%.
card.wonder: Its restless core is linked to two ghostly extra arms of hot gas that ordinary spirals lack.
card.connect: That yardstick reaches straight to the giant Pinwheel, M101, near the Big Dipper’s handle.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows the bright inner spiral; binoculars catch only the core and a hint of the disk.
card.notSee: The spiral arms, and the 'anomalous' arms seen only in hydrogen-alpha, radio and X-ray images.
card.deeper: Reid, Pesce & Riess (2019) modeled VLBI observations of the nuclear water masers to get 7.576 ± 0.082 (stat) ± 0.076 (sys) Mpc, about 1.5% total uncertainty. Cepheids in M106 then anchor the calibration of Type Ia supernova host galaxies, including M101 (SN 2011fe), and hence the Hubble constant. Earlier VLBA work traced about 36 million solar masses inside a fraction of a light-year of the center (SEDS). NASA attributes the anomalous gaseous arms to activity around the central black hole.

card.question: How does a Sun-like star end?
card.answer: Gently, by puffing its outer layers into space, where the hot core left behind lights them up for a brief cosmic moment before everything fades.
card.glance: A tiny, round, even ghost of light, a few arcminutes across, below the bowl of the Big Dipper.
card.whyHere: The Owl Nebula is a Sun-like star’s last breath, lit by the hot core it left behind.
card.see: From Merak, the Big Dipper’s lower pointer star, go about two degrees south-east to a modest star, then just under half a degree east-north-east. Under a dark sky it is at best a faint round smudge; an OIII filter, which passes oxygen’s green glow, helps.
card.understand: When a star like the Sun runs low on fuel, it swells into a red giant and gently sheds its outer layers. The exposed core is small and very hot, and its ultraviolet light makes the gas glow, mostly green from oxygen; the name ‘planetary nebula’ is an old mistake, since no planets are involved. The Owl’s age comes from simple division: the shell’s size, known from Gaia’s distance to the central star, divided by its expansion speed of about 40 kilometers per second, gives roughly ten thousand years.
card.wonder: In a few billion years the Sun will make a shell like this, and anyone watching from 2,600 light-years away might see a ghost just as faint.
card.connect: Stars still on their way to this ending shine across the spring sky, like the pulsing giant R Leonis.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photograph showing the round shell and its two dark 'eyes'; binoculars show at most a faint round spot.
card.notSee: The eyes, the faint outer halo and any color.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 measures a central-star parallax of 1.235 ± 0.046 mas (about 810 pc, 2,640 ly). Guerrero et al. (2003) mapped three shells: an inner shell with a bipolar cavity that produces the eyes, an outer envelope expanding with it at about 40 km/s, and a faint bow-shaped halo slowed by its motion through interstellar gas. Dividing the shell's ~0.4 pc radius by that speed gives a rough kinematic age near 10,000 years; published values span about 6,000–13,000 years because the distance was long uncertain.

card.question: What is that fuzzy ‘star’ between Arcturus and Cor Caroli?
card.answer: A globular cluster, so far out in the galaxy’s halo that hundreds of thousands of ancient stars blend into one soft glow.
card.glance: A round, fuzzy ‘star’ with a brighter center, between Arcturus and Cor Caroli.
card.whyHere: M3 is an ancient ball of hundreds of thousands of stars in the halo around our galaxy.
card.see: Aim a little past halfway from Cor Caroli toward Arcturus. M3 is an obvious round glow, brighter toward the middle, beside a yellowish field star; it will not break into stars in binoculars.
card.understand: A globular cluster is a tight ball of very old stars, and M3 holds about 400,000 Suns’ worth of them. Globulars do not circle in the flat disk with the Sun but loop through a vast halo far above and below it, and M3 is about 33,000 light-years away, farther than the galaxy’s center. Its age, about 12 billion years, comes from the point where its stars begin to swell into giants, which sits among stars lighter than the Sun.
card.wonder: More than two hundred of its stars brighten and fade every half day or so, so the whole cluster flickers.
card.connect: M53, in Coma Berenices, is nearly twice as far and even poorer in heavy elements.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo resolves the outer stars that binoculars blend into haze.
card.notSee: Individual stars: you need a telescope of about 10 cm or more.

(2013) derive 11.75 ± 0.25 Gyr (relative error; systematic uncertainties are larger). Bhardwaj et al. (2020) analyzed 233 RR Lyrae stars in M3, the largest single-cluster sample with near-infrared time series. NASA counts at least 274 variable stars in the cluster.

card.question: How can you tell a star cluster formed very early?
card.answer: By what its stars lack: a cluster this poor in heavy elements must have formed before much of that recycling had happened, more than 12 billion years ago.
card.glance: A small, round glow with a brighter center, about a degree from the star α Comae Berenices.
card.whyHere: M53 is one of the most distant globular clusters in Messier’s catalog, built from nearly pristine gas.
card.see: Find α Comae, at the south-east corner of Coma Berenices between Arcturus and Denebola, and look about one degree north-east. M53 is a compact, round haze with a starlike middle, smaller and fainter than M3.
card.understand: Every element heavier than helium was forged inside stars and spread when they died, so the galaxy’s gas has grown steadily richer, like a soup that thickens as ingredients are added. Spectra of M53’s stars show only about a hundredth of the Sun’s share of these elements. It orbits far out in the halo, roughly as far from the galaxy’s center as it is from us.
card.wonder: The light you see left M53 about 60,000 years ago, during the last Ice Age.
card.connect: A few degrees north-west, M64 is not a cluster in our halo but a whole galaxy, hundreds of times farther away.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo resolves its outer stars; binoculars show a small round glow.
card.notSee: Individual stars and the faint neighbor NGC 5053 (usually).
card.deeper: Baumgardt & Vasiliev (2021): 18.5 ± 0.2 kpc from the Sun and 19.0 kpc from the Galactic Center, with 5.0 × 10⁵ solar masses. Harris (2010): [Fe/H] = −2.10, under one percent of the solar iron fraction. VandenBerg et al. (2013): 12.25 ± 0.25 Gyr. Hubble images show an unusual number of blue stragglers, stars probably rejuvenated by close encounters or mergers in the crowded core (NASA).

card.question: Why does M64’s outer gas circle the wrong way?
card.answer: M64 probably swallowed a smaller, gas-rich galaxy that was orbiting backwards, and where the two streams of gas now meet they collide and set off new stars along the dark dust band.
card.glance: A small oval glow with a noticeably bright, concentrated core.
card.whyHere: The Black Eye Galaxy is a bright spiral in Coma Berenices whose gas does not move the way its stars do.
card.see: M64 lies about seven degrees south-south-west of β Comae, in Coma Berenices between Arcturus and Denebola; use a chart for the last hop. Look for an oval glow with a bright, almost starlike center.
card.understand: The Black Eye is a spiral galaxy roughly 15 to 17 million light-years away. In the early 1990s spectra showed something strange: in the inner region stars and gas orbit one way, while in the outer disk the gas circles the other way. The Doppler shift gives it away, since gas coming toward us looks bluer and gas moving away looks redder, and the pattern flips between the inner and outer disk.
card.wonder: William Herschel already likened its dark patch to a ‘black eye’ in the 1780s.
card.connect: Galaxies grow by swallowing smaller ones, and our own galaxy’s halo carries similar debris.
card.photoCaption: Hubble shows the dark dust band over the core; in binoculars expect a small oval with a bright middle.
card.notSee: The dark dust 'eye' and any sign of the counter-rotating gas.
card.deeper: Red-giant-branch tip distances range from 4.66 Mpc (Jacobs et al. 2009) to 5.27 Mpc (via NED-D). Spectroscopy in the early 1990s showed two nested gas disks rotating in opposite senses: the inner one, with the stars, reaches about 3,000 ly in radius, and the outer counter-rotating one extends to at least 40,000 ly (SEDS). NASA notes that a merger with a satellite galaxy more than a billion years ago is a possible cause.

card.question: Why has M83 had so many supernovae?
card.answer: It makes stars fast, and the heaviest newborn stars live only a few million years before exploding, so a galaxy busy making stars is also busy making supernovae.
card.glance: A large, round, faint glow, low in the south for northern observers and much easier from southern skies.
card.whyHere: M83 is a nearby face-on spiral with six recorded supernovae, a busy star factory you can find in binoculars.
card.see: From mid-northern latitudes it stays low, so catch it due south, well below Spica. Follow a chain of faint stars from γ or π Hydrae to just north of where the two lines meet; in 10×50s it is a soft, round glow with a brighter middle.
card.understand: M83 is a barred spiral, with a straight bar of stars across its center, about 16 million light-years away and seen almost face-on. Its arms are strung with young star clusters and glowing gas clouds where stars are forming fast. Hubble’s wide-field images show the bubbles left by nearly 300 supernovae.
card.wonder: When Lacaille found it from the Cape of Good Hope in 1752, it became the first galaxy discovered beyond our own Local Group.
card.connect: A much older companion of our own galaxy waits nearby in Hydra: the globular cluster M68.
card.photoCaption: Survey photograph of the arms and bar; binoculars show the bright core region as a round glow.
card.notSee: The arms and the pink knots of star formation.

Lacaille's 1752 discovery from the Cape made it the first galaxy found beyond the Local Group (SEDS). Supernovae 1923A, 1945B, 1950B, 1957D, 1968L and 1983N were recorded (SEDS), and Hubble's wide-field images show bubbles from nearly 300 supernovae (NASA). It belongs to a small group with Centaurus A (NGC 5128).

card.question: Is the ring of stars around Polaris a family?
card.answer: The ring is only a lucky arrangement of strangers around the pole.
card.glance: Polaris with a small loop of fainter stars hanging from it, like a diamond set on a ring.
card.whyHere: The Engagement Ring frames Polaris so neatly that it looks designed, which makes it a good test of what counts as a family.
card.see: Find Polaris by following the Big Dipper’s pointer stars, center it, and steady the binoculars against something solid. A loop of faint stars about two Moon-widths across curves away from it, with Polaris sitting on the ring like the gem.
card.understand: The ring is an asterism, a pattern that exists only from our viewpoint. Its stars lie at different distances and travel in different directions. Seen from elsewhere in the galaxy the ring would vanish, just as constellations would.
card.wonder: The ‘diamond’ itself is a supergiant star that gently pulses in brightness.
card.connect: Real star families share an age and a motion, and the Coma Star Cluster is one, slowly coming apart.

card.question: Why does M65 look calm beside its twisted neighbor?
card.answer: It seems to have come through the group’s encounters largely unscathed, a nearly edge-on spiral of older stars, while M66 took the brunt.
card.glance: A faint, thin sliver of light, the western one of Leo’s galaxy pair.
card.whyHere: M65 is a calm spiral in a busy neighborhood, the quiet member of the Leo Triplet.
card.see: Under a dark sky, look below Leo’s hindquarters, between Chertan and ι Leonis. M65 and M66 sit about a third of a degree apart in the same field, two small gray slivers, M65 the narrower and fainter.
card.understand: M65 is a spiral seen nearly edge-on, about 35 million light-years away. Its disk is dominated by older stars and shows little star formation. It also shows little sign of the tidal damage, the stretching by a neighbor’s gravity, so obvious in M66.
card.wonder: Messier missed both galaxies in 1773 while following a comet that passed right between them.
card.connect: M66, in the same field, shows what a neighbor’s pull can do.

card.question: What bent the arms of M66?
card.answer: Its neighbors bent them, for close passes by the other two galaxies of the Leo Triplet have pulled its arms lopsided and its core off-center.
card.glance: A slightly brighter, broader oval glow just east of M65.
card.whyHere: M66 is the brighter, more disturbed member of the Leo Triplet.
card.see: Below Leo’s hindquarters, in the same field as M65, M66 is the brighter of the two, a short oval with a brighter middle. The third member, NGC 3628, is beyond most 50 mm binoculars.
card.understand: M66’s spiral arms are lopsided and its core looks off-center. A neighbor passing close pulls harder on a galaxy’s near side than on its far side and stretches it, the same tidal effect the Moon has on Earth’s oceans. Encounters like this also squeeze gas clouds and set off bursts of star formation.
card.wonder: Five supernovae have been seen in M66 since 1973, a sign of all that fresh star birth.
card.connect: In the Big Dipper, M81 and M82 are another famous interacting pair.

card.question: What is a giant elliptical galaxy?
card.answer: A huge, featureless ball of old stars that has used up its gas, with M49 among the largest nearby.
card.glance: A small, round, evenly bright glow in the empty-looking sky of western Virgo.
card.whyHere: M49 is a giant elliptical galaxy and the first member of the vast Virgo Cluster ever found.
card.see: In western Virgo, between Denebola and Spica, use a chart to hop about six degrees east of the star ο Virginis. Under dark skies M49 is a small round haze, brighter toward the middle, with no structure at all.
card.understand: Elliptical galaxies are smooth swarms of old stars with little gas left to make new ones. M49 is one of the biggest in the cluster, a great city of galaxies about 55 million light-years away. Its distance comes from a statistical trick: the farther a galaxy, the smoother its starlight looks, because more stars blend into each pixel.
card.wonder: About 6,000 globular clusters swarm around M49.
card.connect: Closer to us, the Sombrero is a spiral with a giant bulge of old stars.

card.question: Why is M94 puzzling astronomers?
card.answer: It seems to hold far less dark matter than other spirals, and no one yet knows why.
card.glance: A small, bright, round glow with a starlike center, north of Cor Caroli.
card.whyHere: M94 has a bright ring of newborn stars around its core and a quieter puzzle in its outskirts.
card.see: From Cor Caroli, below the Big Dipper’s handle, move about three degrees north. M94’s compact, bright core makes it one of the easier galaxies here: a fuzzy star wrapped in a soft halo.
card.understand: A wave of star formation has spread outward from M94’s center into a ring where gas is squeezed into new stars. Astronomers weigh a galaxy by how fast its outer parts orbit, as the planets’ speeds weigh the Sun. In most spirals the outskirts move too fast for the visible matter alone, betraying dark matter, the invisible mass that outweighs the stars, but M94’s barely do.
card.wonder: Deep images revealed faint outer arms that roughly triple its known width.
card.connect: Across the border in Coma Berenices, M64 hides another strange inner life.

card.question: Why are the Sunflower’s arms broken into patches?
card.answer: Without a wave to organize it, star formation flickers on patch by patch, and the disk’s rotation smears each patch into a short arc, a sunflower rather than a pinwheel.
card.glance: A faint oval glow with a brighter center, in the northern part of Canes Venatici.
card.whyHere: The Sunflower Galaxy is a spiral whose arms are broken into short patches instead of two clean curves.
card.see: From Cor Caroli, below the Big Dipper’s handle, sweep about five degrees north-east. Under dark skies M63 is a small oval smudge with a brighter middle; the ‘petals’ belong to long-exposure photographs.
card.understand: M63 is a flocculent spiral, its young stars scattered in many short, fluffy arm segments rather than a grand two-armed design. In the Whirlpool, a companion’s pull drives a wave around the disk that herds star birth into two long arms. M63 has no such companion close by.
card.wonder: It was the very first object Pierre Méchain found for Messier’s catalog, in 1779.
card.connect: The Whirlpool, a few degrees away, has crisp arms stirred by a companion.

card.question: How old are the stars of M68?
card.answer: About 12 billion years, close to the age of the universe itself, which makes them among the oldest stars you can see.
card.glance: A small, faint round glow low in the south, in Hydra just below Corvus.
card.whyHere: M68 is an ancient globular cluster made of some of the most metal-poor stars in Messier’s catalog.
card.see: From Kraz, the south-east corner of Corvus south-west of Spica, drop about three and a half degrees south. M68 is a small, faint round haze, and from the north it needs a clear southern horizon.
card.understand: Globular clusters are tight balls of very old stars orbiting through the galaxy’s halo, far from the disk where the Sun lives. M68’s stars hold under one percent of the Sun’s share of heavy elements, so they formed from barely enriched gas. Models of aging stars, fitted to their colors and brightnesses, give the age.
card.wonder: It swings around the galaxy roughly every 400 million years.
card.connect: Hydra also hosts a galaxy where stars are being born at a furious pace: M83.

card.question: How can a dying star’s last breath look like a planet?
card.glance: An 8th-magnitude ‘star’ a couple of degrees south of μ Hydrae that is really the glowing shell of a dying Sun-like star.
card.whyHere: Most dying Sun-like stars are too small or too faint for binoculars, but the Ghost of Jupiter shines brightly enough to find, so you can point to the end of a star’s life even from a suburban sky.
card.see: Find μ Hydrae, a 4th-magnitude star about 16° east-south-east of orange Alphard, and drop about 2° south, a touch west. At 10× the Ghost is an 8th-magnitude point among ordinary stars, and only your chart says which; braced and studied, it may look a shade softer than its neighbors.
card.understand: When a star like the Sun runs out of fuel it swells into a giant and lets its outer layers drift away. The exposed core, on its way to becoming a white dwarf, is so hot that its ultraviolet light makes the shed gas glow, mostly in a green line of oxygen. Gaia’s parallax for that central star puts the shell about 4,400 light-years away.
card.wonder: Its glowing shell is hundreds of times wider than Neptune’s orbit, yet from here it shrinks to a disk no bigger than Jupiter looks.
card.connect: The Eight-Burst Nebula in Vela shows the same ending farther south, with a surprise at its center.
card.answer: In a small telescope its shell shows a round, pale disk close to the size Jupiter appears, hence its name and the misleading term planetary nebula; in binoculars that disk shrinks back into a star.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos show a pale blue-green oval with an inner ‘eye’; binoculars show a starlike point.
card.notSee: No disk, no inner eye and no color in binoculars; a small telescope at about 50× shows the disk.
card.deeper: OpenNGC lists V 7.7 (B 8.6) and a 0.42′ bright inner shell; the central star (V 12.3) has a Gaia parallax of 0.745 mas, about 1.34 kpc, while other estimates reach 4,800 ± 500 light-years. Astronomy magazine finds it 1.8° south of μ Hydrae and describes a 16″ pale blue-green disk in a 4-inch telescope inside a faint 40″ outer shell. William Herschel discovered it in 1785.
